brief.topic: Myth: more agents means a smarter system
brief.audience: PMs and engineers designing agentic systems

coreInsight: Each extra agent adds hand-offs, coordination failures, cost and debugging pain, so start with one agent and split only when an eval shows the split does better.

hooks.text: More agents, more ways to fail.
hooks.notes: Flips the common assumption in five words.

hooks.text: Your multi-agent system might be one agent too many.
Why we merged four agents into one.
hooks.notes: Implies a real case we can’t cite.

selectionRationale: Highest total (23/25): short, contradicts the myth directly, and the reel shows each failure mode then a test for adding an agent.

caption.opening: Multi-agent diagrams look impressive. Every arrow in them is a place where things go wrong.
body:
What each extra agent adds:
→ a hand-off where context gets lost
→ a chance for agents to loop, or confidently agree on the same mistake
→ more model calls, more cost, more waiting
→ one more place to look when something breaks
Start with one agent and a well-defined workflow. Split only when a specific task fails, needs different tools or permissions, and your eval shows the split does better.

claims.text: Adding agents adds hand-off, coordination, cost and debugging overhead; a single agent should be the default until evaluation shows a split performs better.
